promptText: Why must a chat platform resend the entire relevant conversation history on every single request to the model?
options: The model is a stateless prediction function with no persistent memory between calls; continuity is manufactured by the platform re-supplying context each time
Because the model only caches the single most recent message and discards everything else automatically
Because streaming responses technically require the full history to be resubmitted for the connection to stay open
Because Spring AI's ChatMemory abstraction silently deletes history after every call unless resent
explanation: Every request to the model is a cold start; what looks like 'memory' from the user's perspective is really the platform replaying history to a model that starts fresh each time.

promptText: A user opens a browser tab and has two separate topic conversations with the assistant before closing the tab. In this chapter's vocabulary, what does 'session' refer to here?
options: The connection- or auth-level concept (the browser tab) that can span multiple conversations
Each individual back-and-forth exchange between the user and the assistant
The exact same thing as a 'conversation' -- the terms are interchangeable
The database row that stores the persisted chat history
explanation: A turn is one message-reply pair, a conversation is an ordered sequence of turns, and a session is a connection/auth-level concept that may span zero, one, or many conversations -- conflating session with conversation causes real bugs.

promptText: Why do most chat platforms stream tokens as they're generated instead of waiting for the full completion before responding?
options: Perceived latency (time to first token) matters more to user satisfaction than total completion time in most chat UX studies
Streaming reduces the total number of tokens billed by the model provider
Streaming is a mandatory requirement in most model providers' terms of service
Streaming eliminates the need for any input or output guardrail checks
explanation: Design the API and UI around incremental delivery from day one -- users see the first tokens quickly rather than waiting for the entire completion, which drives perceived quality more than total latency.

promptText: Why should a conversation ID be an opaque, unguessable UUID rather than a predictable sequential integer?
options: A predictable ID adds risk if ownership checks are ever weak or missing, since a guessable ID lowers the bar for accessing another user's conversation
Sequential integers cannot technically be indexed efficiently by any relational database
UUIDs are a hard requirement of Spring Data JPA for any primary key
UUIDs are needed specifically to make Server-Sent Events function correctly
explanation: Making the ID unguessable is defense-in-depth layered on top of the real control -- an explicit ownership/authorization check enforced on every read and write, not the ID's unguessability alone.

promptText: What operational factor most often drives choosing Server-Sent Events (SSE) over WebSockets for a single-user chat product?
options: SSE rides over plain HTTP, working through existing load balancers, proxies, and CDNs with far less infrastructure change, and degrades gracefully
WebSockets are fundamentally incapable of transmitting plain text data
SSE natively supports full bidirectional communication while WebSockets do not
SSE connections are inherently more encrypted than WebSocket connections
explanation: The deciding factors are usually operational: SSE needs less infrastructure change and degrades gracefully, while WebSockets buy bidirectionality at the cost of connection-aware load balancing and more careful proxy handling.

promptText: In Spring AI's role-tagged message model for a conversation, who is meant to control the content of the 'system' role message?
options: The platform, never the end user directly
The end user, since it should reflect their personal preferences
The model itself, since it generates system messages as part of its reasoning
Whichever party sent the most recent message in the conversation
explanation: The system role carries standing instructions -- persona, constraints, safety boundaries -- and is controlled by the platform, distinct from the user role which carries untrusted end-user input.

promptText: Which statement correctly compares the memory-shaping strategies (sliding window, rolling summary, retrieval over history) this chapter describes?
options: A sliding window is cheap and preserves exact wording for recent turns but can cause amnesia about anything only mentioned in dropped turns; rolling summarization preserves long-range facts more cheaply but can lose nuance and adds its own recurring model-call cost
Retrieval over history requires no additional infrastructure and is always the cheapest option at any conversation length
A sliding window scales indefinitely with zero risk of amnesia, regardless of window size
Rolling summarization eliminates all token cost growth for free, with no added latency or model calls
explanation: Each strategy trades off differently between the amnesia and overflow failure modes; rolling summarization specifically adds its own background model-call cost that must be measured as a real line item, not assumed free.

promptText: A user's send request times out client-side and they click Send again. What mechanism does the chapter recommend to avoid the message being processed twice?
options: The client generates an idempotency key per send attempt, reused on retry; the server checks whether it already accepted or completed a request with that key before creating a new message
The server should deduplicate purely by comparing the text similarity of recent messages
The client should be forced to wait a fixed 10 seconds before any retry is allowed
The model itself should recognize it already answered an identical-looking question
explanation: This is the same idempotency-key pattern used in payment APIs, applied to chat sends, because a client-side timeout doesn't reveal whether the server actually received and processed the original request.

promptText: Why is a system prompt, on its own, insufficient to prevent prompt injection in a multi-turn chat platform?
options: The system prompt is just more text inside the same context window as user input and replayed history, with no hard mechanism to make the model treat it as categorically different, especially many turns deep in a conversation
Model providers automatically strip the system prompt after the first turn of any conversation
System prompts are limited to 50 tokens by every major provider, making them too short to be effective
Prompt injection can only ever occur in the very first message of a conversation
explanation: Because the system prompt competes with untrusted content in the same context, real protection requires layered controls -- input/output moderation, structural separation, and least-privilege tool design -- not prompt wording alone.

promptText: What must correctly implementing a 'stop generation' button guarantee, according to the chapter?
options: The cancellation signal must propagate down to actually abort the in-flight model API call, so tokens genuinely stop being generated and billed, not merely stop being forwarded to the client
Simply closing the client connection is sufficient and unambiguous as a stop signal
The partial response already produced should always be discarded rather than persisted
Stopping generation should also delete the user's original message from history
explanation: Most provider SDKs support aborting an in-flight streaming request; without propagating cancellation, the server keeps consuming and paying for tokens even after the client stops listening.

promptText: Using Little's Law (L = lambda x W) for a streaming chat platform, if the user base doubles while the average time each request spends being generated stays the same, what happens to the number of concurrent in-flight generations?
options: It roughly doubles too, directly increasing the concurrency your infrastructure and provider limits must support
It stays constant, since streaming inherently amortizes load across users
It decreases due to caching effects on repeated prompts
It becomes fundamentally unpredictable and cannot be estimated using Little's Law
explanation: L = lambda x W is arithmetic: doubling arrival rate lambda while holding time-in-system W constant doubles the average concurrent in-flight generations L, which capacity planning must account for explicitly.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend keeping the usage/rate-limit store (e.g., Redis) architecturally separate from the durable conversation store (e.g., Postgres or DynamoDB)?
options: Rate limiting needs to be extremely fast and is naturally a counter/TTL problem, while conversation history needs to be durable and queryable -- fundamentally different storage shapes for different access patterns
Regulations require any AI feature to use at least two physically separate databases
Combining them would make horizontal scaling of the chat service technically impossible
Redis is architecturally incapable of storing any text content, only numeric counters
explanation: Conflating the two into one store is a common early mistake that becomes painful to unwind once traffic grows, since the two workloads have genuinely different performance and durability requirements.

promptText: A user's WiFi drops mid-stream and reconnects seconds later. Why does the chapter treat immediately cancelling the server-side generation on disconnect as a mistake, and what should happen instead?
options: Generation should keep running server-side, decoupled from any one client connection, with tokens persisted or buffered so the client can resume on reconnect -- cancelling immediately wastes already-paid-for work if the user reconnects shortly after
Cancelling immediately is correct because continuing to generate for a disconnected client always wastes tokens with no possible benefit
The platform should require the user to manually retype and resend the exact same message after every reconnect
No special handling is needed since HTTP automatically resumes any dropped stream from where it left off
explanation: Decoupling 'is the model still generating' from 'is this specific client connection alive' lets the server persist tokens and let the client resume rather than losing in-progress work on a brief network blip.

promptText: A user edits an earlier message in a long conversation and resubmits. Why does the chapter recommend modeling the conversation as a tree with parent pointers instead of overwriting everything that came after the edited message?
options: Editing effectively creates a new branch; modeling the conversation as a tree keeps both the original and edited branches retrievable, so users can compare or revert rather than permanently losing the original path
Overwriting subsequent messages is correct because only one conversation path can ever exist at a time
The entire conversation should be deleted and a brand new one started whenever any message is edited
Only the edited message should be kept, discarding all prior history to save storage
explanation: Rather than destroying data, well-designed platforms give each message a parent pointer so both branches remain retrievable, even though only one branch is 'active' at a time for continued conversation.

promptText: A platform serves both free-tier consumer traffic and enterprise customers with SLAs on shared infrastructure. Why is per-user rate limiting alone insufficient to protect enterprise customers during a sudden free-tier traffic spike?
options: Per-user limits cap individual users but don't stop an aggregate free-tier burst from consuming a shared capacity pool, degrading latency for enterprise traffic; true isolation requires separate resource pools or priority queuing, not just per-user limits
Per-user rate limiting is actually fully sufficient on its own and no further isolation is ever needed
The correct fix is simply giving enterprise customers unlimited rate limits to compensate for any contention
The only real solution is over-provisioning compute for 100% of theoretical worst-case peak load at all times
explanation: This is the same noisy-neighbor problem multi-tenant infrastructure always has, applied to LLM inference capacity -- resolved by resource-pool isolation or priority queuing, not by rate limits alone.
